newsitem.title: USA: SPORT - GOLF'S WOODS ON HIS PRO CAREER - AUG 13.
newsitem.headline: SPORT - GOLF'S WOODS ON HIS PRO CAREER - AUG 13.

text.p: Last year at this time, Tiger Woods was preparing for his assault on a record- setting third straight U.S. Amateur golf title.

Now Woods is balancing new demands, expectations and responsibilities from a career that has produced six pro titles including an historic 12-shot win at the Masters, endorsement deals worth about $100 million and hero worship from a new generation of golf fans.
"This time last year I was getting ready for the U.S. Am, and that seems like about 10 years ago for some reason," the 21-year-old Woods said Tuesday. "My life has changed a lot."

There has been a downside for Woods, who told a news conference ahead of the PGA Championship starting Thursday that he can't afford to have bad days in public -- the price he's paid for his fabulous success and the riches that came with it.

"That's one thing I've come to understand and had to learn at a very young age. When most people wake up in the morning and wake up on the wrong side of bed and they're in a grumpy mood and just unhappy with life, they can go out and they can say things and be okay with it.
"Unfortunately, I can't do that. I can't afford to have those kind of days in public and that's one of the things that has been hard to handle. And I've had to learn."

After Woods's one-sided romp at Augusta National, where he became the youngest and first black champion and winner by the largest margin ever at the Masters, visions of an unprecedented modern Grand Slam sweep abounded and expectations soared.

"Augusta was one of those once in a lifetime experiences when you play that well, and it happened to be in a major," he said. "I was lucky enough to have everything gel together for 63 holes (after a struggling opening nine) in a major."
What followed was perhaps less fortunate for Woods.

"I've gone through a lot of experiences and I've been more than anything forced to grow up and very quickly because some of the issues I've been forced to handle are issues and things that you should handle a little bit later, like in the mid or late-20s.

"Whether it's the media spotlight or recognition of being out in public. Being on the road, living away from home for the first time, permanently. These are new experiences and I've had to adjust and learn very quickly."
Woods, however, is a quick study and says that overall, "I've had a lot of fun."

The charismatic American has also engaged in a crash course on Winged Foot itself from his swing coach Butch Harmon, who grew up playing on the classic layout where his father served for 31 years as the club professional.

"This has been an unbelievable break for me because obviously it's my first PGA. He's helped me on the greens, especially telling me things that only locals would know," Woods said. "Putts break certain ways -- you got to believe it, you got to trust it. And he's right.

"He's played here for 25 years so I think he knows a few things. He's talking about some of the wind conditions which can happen, prevailing winds. Some holes play a little shorter than others. Some are more deceiving off the tees. This is invaluable knowledge to have, and I'm very lucky."
Woods also sounded relieved that some of the spotlight has been taken off him after the victories by Ernie Els in the U.S. Open and Justin Leonard at the British.
"I do think there's less attention," he said. "You've got Justin and Ernie and Colin (Montgomerie) and a lot of players playing well right now."
That doesn't mean Woods should be overlooked despite falling short of his own high standards at the last two majors.

"As far as my performance in the other two majors, I just made too many mistakes. At the U.S. Open (tied 19th) I didn't drive the ball particularly well. It is awfully tough to play the U.S. Open when you're not driving the ball well.

"And then at the British (tied 24th), I actually played pretty good. I just had three bad holes (a quadruple bogey and two triples). And if you take those three holes away and you put pars on the card, I finished second."
The power of positive thinking from golf's most powerful new star. REUTER 122341 GMT aug 97
